title: Cap. XI: Placeus alien from Pelagian, Socinian, and Remonstrant teaching
pass_a_gloss: Chapter XI. That Placeus is foreign to the opinion of the Pelagians, Socinians, and Remonstrants in this matter. So that he may render us hated and overwhelm us with the heaviest prejudices, it grieves him that we make common cause with the Pelagians and Socinians. But there is no cause for grieving: for we shrink from the errors of such men as much as anyone. He adds that the opinion of the most ancient heretics (I take it the Marcionites and the Manichees, who with the height of impiety asserted that the ancient law was evil) was that there can be no just imputation of another's sin. What does this have to do with the matter?
pass_b_english: Chapter XI. That Placeus stands apart from the Pelagian, Socinian, and Remonstrant teaching on this question. Garissoles wants to make us hated and crush us under the heaviest prejudices by grieving that we make common cause with Pelagians and Socinians. There is nothing to grieve over. We shrink from the errors of such men as strongly as anyone can. He adds that the oldest heretics — I take him to mean the Marcionites and the Manichees, who with the height of impiety called the old law evil — held that there can be no just imputation of another's sin. What does that have to do with our question?
source_text: CAPUT XI. A Pelagianorum, Socinianorum, & Remonstrantium in hoc negotio sententia Placeum esse alienum. Ut nos reddat exosos, & gravissimis obruat praejudiciis, dolet nos cum Pelagianis & Socinianis paria facere. Sed dolendi causa nulla est: Nam ab hujusmodi hominum erroribus abhorremus, ut qui maxime. Vetustissimorum, addit, haereticorum (Marcionitas puto, & Manicheos, qui legem antiquam malam esse summa cum impietate afferebant) sententia fuit, nullam esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem. Quid hoc ad rem?
